extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of drama/literary criticism; playwrights and critics studying Aristotle's Poetics and tragic theory
extracted.subtask_short: Aristotelian tragedy and tragic hero analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria from a literary-critical textbook chapter on Aristotle's Poetics about dramatic unities, the function of tragedy, and the nature of the ideal tragic hero. Useful for evaluating or composing tragedies according to classical/aesthetic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action as primary law
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Unity of Action is the higher and controlling law of the drama.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drama should be governed above all by a single, coherent action. Other rules (e.g., Time and Place) are of secondary and derivative value and must not be allowed to subordinate or fracture the central plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unities of Time and Place are secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unities of Time and Place, so far as they can claim any artistic importance, are of secondary and purely derivative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict observance of Time and Place can harm the inner logic of character and event (e.g., compressing incidents into twelve or twenty-four hours, or preventing characters from moving to where dramatic motives demand), and should be subordinated to Unity of Action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama requires idealisation of place and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is not possible without a certain idealisation of place and time; the poet 'transports us to a far-off land and a distant age' and we do not insist on clock-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may span long intervals between acts or compress/expand time if the poet's art justifies it; the audience forgives temporal liberties when the imaginative world is coherent and demands are made by a skilled artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of tragedy: produce katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis of pity and fear; pity being felt for a person who, if not wholly innocent, meets with suffering beyond his deserts; fear being awakened when the sufferer is a man of like nature with ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots and characters must be arranged to evoke these emotions — pity for undeserved suffering and fear stemming from recognisable human likeness — so that the tragic effect is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must be neither eminently good nor utterly bad
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic character should be 'not eminently good or just, though he leans to the side of goodness' and 'morally stands midway between the two extremes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protagonist of mixed moral quality invites pity and fear; extremes (perfect virtue or utter depravity) fail to generate both emotions properly and so are unsuitable as the central tragic figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist should be illustrious in rank/fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: He is, moreover, illustrious in rank and fortune; the chief motive being that the signal nature of the catastrophe may be more strikingly exhibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High social standing or prominence heightens the impact of the fall and makes the catastrophe more dramatically effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downfall should arise from a great flaw or error (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disaster that wrecks his life may be traced not to deliberate wickedness, but to some great flaw of character or fatal error in conduct (dpaptia/hamartia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia may be an intellectual error, a moral frailty, a defect of character, or an act in passion; it need not be voluntary vice. The single great error or defect should be causally connected to the tragic outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia's shades: intellectual error, moral frailty, or defect of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Dpaptia admits various meanings: error from inadequate knowledge (intellectual), an act in passion (adixnpa), or a more permanent defect of character distinct from vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret hamartia broadly: it can be a culpable mistake due to ignorance, an unintentional error of judgment, a passion-driven act, or a character flaw; what matters is that it plausibly leads to catastrophe and elicits pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude perfectly blameless victims as tragic heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectacle of a man eminently good undergoing change from prosperous to adverse fortune 'dawkens neither pity nor fear. It shocks or repels us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wholly blameless victims tend to provoke moral indignation or admiration rather than the mixed pity-and-fear appropriate to tragedy; such themes are often judged unsuitable for pure tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the wicked who prosper
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of the bad man who experiences the change from distress to prosperity is utterly devoid of tragic quality; 'pity and fear are here alike wanting' and it offends the sense of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting the wicked rewarded undermines tragic effect and introduces aesthetic and moral disturbance rather than the harmonised cause-effect expected in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overthrow of the utter villain lacks true tragic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The overthrow of the utter villain 'satisfies the moral sense, but is lacking in the higher and distinctively tragic qualities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment of obvious villainy gratifies justice but does not typically produce pity and fear; such outcomes are not sufficient for classic tragic catharsis unless accompanied by other tragic elements or complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unhappy (tragic) ending is central
rubrics_metrics.description: The stress laid in this chapter on the unhappy ending is the key to Aristotle's preference: the true tragic ending produces the proper tragic effect; a happy ending belongs to comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should culminate in disaster or an unhappy resolution that restores moral order through loss; attempts to convert tragic plots to happy endings change their genre and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should produce its effect by reading as well as performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires a good tragedy to produce its proper effect merely by reading; Euripides' powerful tragic effect is partly stage-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play's tragic power should not rely entirely on spectacle or acting; the literary structure — plot, character, and thought — must convey catharsis in the text itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic character needs motive power and self-assertive energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic character implies some self-assertive energy; it is not rounded or perfect but presses forward passionately in a single direction; pure goodness tends to be immobile and uncombative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists should have drive and agency that produce decisive acts, impel others, and generate collisions of forces essential to drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and paired characters (light and shade)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider law demands the light and shade of contrasted characters—characters either standing out against one another in strong relief, or each forming the complement of the other (e.g., Antigone and Ismene, Hamlet and Laertes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cast of contrasting ethical types deepens dramatic interest and supports the tragic structure; 'gratuitously bad' characters may be allowed when required by dramatic motive and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: True tragic collision: character/passion can determine destiny
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'true tragic collision' is one in which character and passion determine destiny; the great frailty will then be a moral frailty and the collision will often be internal (conscience, divided will) or provoked by encroachment on a sphere not his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective tragedy can arise from internal moral struggle as well as external fate; drama should show how an initial flaw or choice implicitly contains its tragic outcome, uniting beginning and end causally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of villainy can produce tragic awe when portrayed with genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Wickedness on a grand scale, resolute and intellectual, may raise the criminal above the commonplace and invest him with a sort of dignity; the wreck of such power excites a certain tragic sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Aristotle warns against centring tragedy on utter depravity, exceptional portrayals (e.g., Richard III.) can elicit terror/awe and quasi-tragic sympathy if the villain is rendered with commanding complexity—this requires exceptional dramatic skill.
